title: The bugle horn, counting rests and first transposing
summary: Dawson moves him to the bugle horn, teaches him to count rests, and transposing piano parts for it is his first arranging.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: At first he asked me, "Would you like to play another horn?" I said, "Yes!" I'm in the band; I'm playin' my cymbals. So he looked over there, and he had a bugle horn. He said, "Would you like to play that?" Anything! Because I'm so glad he didn't pick up a clarinet, because them clarinets are so hard to play.

So he gave me the bugle horn. And I guess he must have gave me a book, you know, with the fingering. And after a few sessions with the bugle horn, and after I'd got a little embrochure... That was easy, because usually when you're reading the bugle horn, it really doesn't teach you how to read, because so many times you have a rest... He taught us how to... He's the first one that taught me how to count a rest out. He said, "You count... You've got four bars. You say, 'one-two-three-four,' 'two-two-three-four,' 'three-two-three-four,' 'four-two-three-four,' BOOM." And I just carried that over later on, because if you keep putting that next number after every bar, you'll know how far it is. But if you just start counting, you know...
So he taught you guys how to count.
Right. So I got to fool with this bugle horn. And he explained to me that the bugle horn was the third to... I had a feeling that I wanted to play something with

the piano. So he said with the bugle horn, you transpose a third down, a minor third down. And when he showed that to me, that was an easy transposition, because if a note is on the second line on the piano, your note will be on the first line for you. The only thing that you have to change is the signature. It don't (?). And it's funny about how that makes a note, even when you... If you've got an A-flat, your note will be F-natural. And if you've got an A-natural, your note will be F-sharp; you've got to make the tone(?) there. So that classification was easy. And do you know, I started transposing piano parts so I could play my bugle horn along with the piano? And when I think about it, that's when I first got involved with arranging.
